title: Anatomical and Directional Medical Terminology

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of 'anterior' like the front cover of a book - it is the side you see first when someone faces you. Your belly button and nose are on your anterior side. The opposite, the back cover, is 'posterior.' So when a term says anterior, picture the front.

### Question 2

Imagine a line drawn straight down the middle of your body, right through your nose and belly button. 'Medial' means closer to that middle line. Your nose sits closer to the middle than your ears do, so your nose is medial to your ears. The word 'median,' like the strip in the middle of a road, can help you remember 'middle.'

### Question 3

Think of your arm like a tree branch growing from the trunk. The part 'proximal' is the part closest to where the branch joins the trunk - near your shoulder. The word sounds like 'proximity,' which means being close by. So proximal = close to the body.

### Question 4

When you look at a friend standing across from you and they raise their right hand, it appears on your left side, like looking in a mirror. To avoid confusion, doctors always mean the patient's own left and right, not what the person looking at them sees. That way everyone talks about the same side.

### Question 5

Think of the Earth: the grass on top is 'superficial' (on the surface), and the hot core buried far inside is 'deep.' In your body, your skin is superficial and your bones are deep. The words describe how far in or out something is, not up, down, or sideways.

### Question 6

For arms and legs, we have special words: 'proximal' means closer to where the limb attaches to the body, and 'distal' means farther away. The knee is closer to the hip than the ankle is, so the knee is proximal. It is like measuring along a garden hose from where it screws into the faucet.

### Question 7

Imagine everyone agreed that on a map, north is always up. Then no matter how you turn, 'north' means the same direction. Anatomical position is that agreed starting pose for the body, so 'front' and 'up' always mean the same body parts even if the person is lying down or flipped over.

### Question 8

Break the phrase into two clues: 'posterior' means the back side, and 'distal' means the far end away from the body. So for a leg, that is the back part, down near the ankle - like the bottom back of a candy cane rather than the top hook.

### Question 9

Picture your body from the side: your lungs are up in your chest, and your stomach is below them in your belly. 'Inferior' just means lower down toward the feet. So the stomach being inferior to the lungs simply means it sits lower than the lungs - which is exactly right.

### Question 10

Coming in from the front means an 'anterior' approach. As the surgeon cuts inward from the skin to the organ, they move from the outside (superficial) toward the inside (deep), like digging from the surface of the ground down toward something buried. Two clues together: from the front, and from outside toward inside.

### Question 11

'Anterior' is glued to your belly side forever - it never changes which body part it means. If you lie face down, your belly still faces the floor, so your anterior side just points down at the table now. The word stays with the front of you no matter which way you flip.

### Question 12

The prefix 'ipsi-' means 'same,' and 'contra-' means 'against' or 'opposite,' like the word 'contradict.' So your right hand and right foot are on the same side (ipsilateral), while your right hand and left foot are on opposite sides (contralateral). Match the prefixes to same versus opposite.
